Respiratory & Musculoskeletal

Two systems with heavy dental overlap: sinusitis mistaken for toothache, sleep apnoea a dentist can screen and treat, MRONJ and osteoradionecrosis of the jaw, and TMD.

01

Structure and control of respiration

The tract, the chemoreceptors, and the non-respiratory jobs.

Upper

Upper respiratory tract

  • Nose & nasal cavity — warms, humidifies, filters air
  • Sinuses — resonance + mucus production
  • Pharynx — shared passage for air and food
  • Larynx — airway protection + phonation
Lower

Lower respiratory tract

  • Trachea — C-shaped cartilage rings
  • Bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli

Control of respiration

  1. Central chemoreceptors (medulla)
    Located in the medullary respiratory centres; the primary drivers of ventilation. Respond to ↑ CO2 and ↑ H+ in cerebrospinal fluid, regulating minute-to-minute rate and depth.
  2. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid & aortic bodies)
    Respond principally to falling oxygen.
CO2 drives breathing, not O2

The primary drivers are the central chemoreceptors responding to CO2 and H+. Oxygen sensing is peripheral and secondary. This matters in COPD, where chronic CO2 retention blunts the central response and the patient becomes more dependent on hypoxic drive — which is why high-flow oxygen needs care in these patients.

Non-respiratory functions

Defence against noxious atmospheric substances Synthesis, release and metabolism of bradykinin, serotonin, some prostaglandins Angiotensin I → angiotensin II by pulmonary endothelial cells

Respiratory epithelium

Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium lines the trachea and bronchi. It gives the appearance of multiple layers, but all cells contact the basement membrane. Cilia beat in a coordinated upward motion → mucociliary clearance, which is vital for removing inhaled particles.

Mucociliary clearance is the recurring casualty

Impaired mucociliary clearance appears again in sinusitis, in COPD, and in cystic fibrosis. Damage the escalator and inhaled material stays — which is the common first step in most of the diseases below.

02

Classifying respiratory disease and its symptoms

The categories, and what each symptom actually means.

GroupConditions
Upper respiratory tractInfections, sinusitis
Lower respiratory tractAcute bronchitis, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, asthma, COPD (chronic bronchitis and emphysema), cystic fibrosis, pulmonary embolism, granulomatous disease

Each may be acute or chronic.

Common clinical problems

Symptom 1

Cough

The most common respiratory symptom — dry, productive or paroxysmal. Causes include viral infection, asthma, chronic bronchitis, pneumonia, reflux, lung cancer. Persistent cough (>3 weeks) warrants investigation.

Symptom 2

Dyspnoea

The sensation of breathlessness — graded by the exertion needed to provoke it.

Pathological basis of two key signs

Purulent sputumThick, yellow–green sputum indicating a neutrophil-rich exudate; suggests bacterial infection — bronchitis, pneumonia, bronchiectasis
HaemoptysisBlood in sputum, from streaks to frank blood; causes include ulceration of mucosa, tumour, infection and infarction
Two red flags

Cough persisting beyond 3 weeks and haemoptysis both warrant investigation. In a smoker these carry particular weight — lung cancer is on the list of causes for both.

Major aetiological factors

GeneticCystic fibrosis → defective CFTR protein → thick mucus, recurrent infections, bronchiectasis. α-1 antitrypsin deficiency → unopposed neutrophil elastase → early-onset emphysema
InfectionViral (influenza, RSV, rhinovirus) → acute illness and exacerbations
α-1 antitrypsin explains emphysema mechanistically

Antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase. Without it, elastase digests alveolar elastic tissue unopposed — producing emphysema in a young non-smoker. Smoking does the same thing by a different route: it recruits neutrophils and inactivates antitrypsin. Same end point, inherited or acquired.

From the lecture slides
03

Sinusitis

The respiratory condition most likely to reach you first.

  • Inflammation of the epithelial lining of the paranasal sinuses
  • Causes mucosal oedema and increase in mucosal secretions
  • Major organisms: streptococci, staphylococci, pneumococci and Haemophilus influenzae
  • Often confused with migraine, and vice versa

Oral manifestations and the diagnostic problem

It cuts both ways

The proximity of maxillary teeth and the superior alveolar nerve to the maxillary antrum can mimic pain of dental origin. Conversely, roughly 25% of maxillary sinusitis cases are associated with dental infections or causes.

So sinusitis can present as toothache, and toothache can cause sinusitis. Neither diagnosis excludes the other.

Distinguishing features to test

Movement of head Vitality testing Palpation / percussion
The three tests, and why they work

Movement of the head — sinus pain characteristically worsens on bending forward, dental pain does not. Vitality testing — sinusitis does not devitalise teeth, so multiple vital teeth with diffuse upper pain points away from a dental cause. Percussion — sinusitis often makes several adjacent maxillary teeth tender, whereas a periapical lesion localises to one.

A patient reports aching in several upper posterior teeth, worse on bending forward. All test vital. What are you thinking?

Maxillary sinusitis rather than a dental cause. The proximity of maxillary teeth and the superior alveolar nerve to the maxillary antrum can mimic pain of dental origin, and the pattern fits: multiple teeth involved, all vital, and pain provoked by movement of the head. But do not stop there — roughly 25% of maxillary sinusitis is associated with dental infections or causes, so still look for an odontogenic source.

From the lecture slides
04

COPD

Chronic bronchitis and emphysema — irreversible obstruction.

COPD

Chronic disease resulting in difficulty in exhalation / expiration of air. Consists of two major diseases — chronic bronchitis and emphysema — both characterised by chronic airflow obstruction during normal ventilatory efforts.

Pathogenesis

  1. Impaired mucociliary clearance
    The escalator fails.
  2. Irritation causing thickened hypersecretion
    More mucus, harder to move.
  3. Damaged fibroelastic tissue
    Loss of the elastic recoil that drives expiration.
  4. Impaired inflammatory response and airway wall thickening
    Oedema and fibrosis.
  5. Irreversible narrowing of the bronchial airway
    And with it, diminished gaseous exchange leading to hypoxaemia.
Why expiration is the problem

Inspiration is active — muscles pull air in. Expiration is largely passive, driven by elastic recoil. Destroy the fibroelastic tissue and there is nothing to push air back out, so air is trapped. That is why COPD is defined by difficulty in expiration.

Oral manifestations and dental management

Smoking-related oral lesions such as melanosis, nicotine stomatitis, and dysplastic changes of the oral mucosa.

  1. Preserve respiratory capacity during treatment
     
  2. A more upright chair position
    Supine positioning worsens breathlessness.
  3. Refrain from CNS-depressing drugs
    They further blunt respiratory drive.
  4. High flow of O2 can be needed
    But with the caution above about CO2 retention.
The oral lesions are a shared-risk-factor story

Nicotine stomatitis and dysplastic mucosal change are not caused by COPD — they share its cause. A COPD patient is by definition a long-duration smoker, which places them squarely in the high-risk group from L7C, where duration matters most.

From the lecture slides
05

Asthma

The reversible one.

Asthma

An intermittent respiratory disorder characterised by airway hyperactivity to various stimuli. It produces recurrent bronchial smooth muscle spasm, inflammation and swelling of bronchial mucosa, hypersecretion of viscid mucus and sputum plugging. 11% prevalence in Australia; all ages but more common in children.

Pathogenesis

Not dissimilar to chronic bronchitis — however, there is a REVERSIBLE component. Airway wall thickening, thickened mucous hypersecretion, and alveolar gas trapping.

Reversibility is the whole distinction

COPD produces irreversible narrowing; asthma has a reversible component. That single difference is why asthma responds to bronchodilators and why the two are managed differently, despite overlapping pathology.

Asthma attack

Wheezing Coughing Cyanosis Perspiration Tachycardia Chest tightness

Inhaled medications

  • Bronchodilators — administered directly to the region requiring treatment; integral in relief of acute symptoms and complementary in long-term management
  • Beta-2 adrenergic agonists (salbutamol — Ventolin) — the most commonly prescribed drugs for preventing asthmatic attacks, acting on airway smooth muscle
Inhalers and the mouth

Lecture 6 covered the oral consequences: inhaled corticosteroids predispose to erythematous candidosis and median rhomboid glossitis, and the first-line management includes rinsing the mouth after using steroid inhalers. An asthmatic patient with a sore red tongue is a recognisable picture.

In the surgery

Ask an asthmatic patient to bring their reliever inhaler and keep it accessible during treatment. Anxiety, and in susceptible patients aspirin or NSAIDs, can provoke an attack.

From the lecture slides
06

Obstructive sleep apnoea

A respiratory disorder a dentist can help treat.

Obstructive sleep apnoea

A sleep disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of narrowing or collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep despite ongoing breathing efforts, often leading to acute derangement in blood gases.

Three types of sleep apnoea

Central (5–10%)Decrease in ventilatory drive
ObstructiveApnoea = a drop in peak signal excursion by ≥90% of pre-event baseline, lasting ≥10 seconds. Hypopnoea is a lesser reduction with desaturation or arousal
MixedFeatures of both

Why it matters

The combination of low oxygen levels and broken sleep causes symptoms and associations including:

Excessive daytime sleepiness Snoring Cardiovascular disease Cerebrovascular disease Diabetes Depression Brain damage

Screening and diagnosis

  • Snoring is a symptom, not a problem in and of itself — but should be taken seriously as a sign of a very serious underlying problem
  • 1 in 5 adults have mild OSA; 1 in 15 have moderate to severe OSA
  • 80% of those with OSA remain undiagnosed
  • Screening questionnaires: STOP-BANG, Epworth
80% undiagnosed — and the signs are in the mouth

Structural: narrow palate, retrognathia, deviated septum, thickened soft palate, large uvula, large tonsils. Signs: parafunction, scalloped tongue, Mallampati score, oral dryness at night. A dentist examines every one of these routinely, which makes dentistry a realistic screening point for a condition four in five sufferers do not know they have.

Treatment

First line

CPAP

The current gold standard and first-line management. Acts as a pneumatic splint preventing nocturnal collapse of the upper airway. Improves quality of life, sleepiness, neuropsychological performance and hypertension. Main limitation: poor compliance.

Second line

Oral appliances (MAS/MAD)

Stabilise the airway preventing collapsibility; widen the lateral airway, particularly the velopharyngeal region; anteriorly displace the tongue. Many designs, and improved compliance compared with CPAP.

Other options: upper airway surgery, stimulators and weight loss. All options have a place in the management of OSA.

Side effects of MAS/MAD to warn about

Jaw discomfort or pain, TMJ discomfort, changes in tooth alignment or bite, excessive salivation, dry mouth, soreness of teeth or gums, throat dryness, tension headaches — and in some cases increased snoring or exacerbation of sleep apnoea. Bite change is the one patients are least prepared for and most bothered by, so consent for it explicitly.

CPAP is more effective than an oral appliance. Why is a mandibular advancement splint still a reasonable choice?

Because effectiveness in trials is not effectiveness in use. CPAP is the gold standard and first-line therapy, but its major limitation is poor compliance. Oral appliances have improved compliance, and a device that is worn every night may deliver more real benefit than a superior device that is not. The lecture is explicit that all options have a place.

07

Bone biology and remodelling

A living tissue, and the cycle that maintains it.

Bone is a highly dynamic, metabolically active tissue, not a static structural material. At any time, millions of microscopic bone remodelling units are active throughout the skeleton, continuously replacing old or damaged bone. Remodelling is a lifelong process.

Four functions

Structural support and load bearing Protection of organs Mineral homeostasis Haemopoiesis

Two forms of bone

Cortical

Compact bone

The dense outer shell and shafts of long bones. Highly organised into Haversian systems; mechanically strong; slower turnover.

Trabecular

Cancellous bone

Internal lattice; high surface area; metabolically more active and therefore affected earlier by metabolic bone disease.

Three cells

OsteoblastsDerived from mesenchymal stem cells; form bone
OsteoclastsDerived from the monocyte–macrophage lineage; resorb bone
OsteocytesFormer osteoblasts embedded in matrix; sense mechanical strain and signal for remodelling

The remodelling cycle

  1. Activation
    Signals such as microdamage or altered loading recruit a basic multicellular unit.
  2. Resorption
    Osteoclasts remove old or damaged bone.
  3. Reversal
    Transition from resorption to formation.
  4. Formation
    Osteoblasts lay down new matrix, which mineralises.
Coupling is the concept that explains the diseases

Resorption and formation are normally coupled — balanced within each unit. Osteoporosis is uncoupling in one direction (resorption exceeds formation). MRONJ results from suppressing resorption so far that the whole cycle stalls. Both diseases below are coupling failures.

Pathological basis of bone pain

Importantly, the mineralised matrix itself is not innervated — pain originates from associated structures. Mechanisms include periosteal stretching (the periosteum is richly innervated), inflammation, fracture, tumour infiltration and pathologically increased pressure.

Why that matters clinically

Because the matrix is not innervated, a lesion can destroy a great deal of bone painlessly until it reaches or stretches the periosteum. That is part of why bone pathology can present late — and why radiographic change may precede symptoms.

From the lecture slides
08

Osteoporosis, MRONJ and ORN

Three bone conditions with direct dental consequences.

Osteoporosis

  • Metabolic bone disease characterised by reduced bone mass, with normal mineralisation of the remaining bone
  • Results in increased risk of fragility fractures
  • Pathogenesis: uncoupling of bone remodelling — bone resorption exceeds bone formation — with progressive net bone loss over time
Reduced mass, normal mineral

That phrase distinguishes osteoporosis from osteomalacia. In osteoporosis there is less bone, of normal quality. In osteomalacia there is normal quantity, poorly mineralised. Same fragility, different mechanism.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ)

An adverse effect of anti-resorptive medications, used in osteoporosis and in oncology patients to prevent bone metastases. Most commonly associated with bisphosphonates (e.g. pamidronate, zoledronate) and denosumab; less commonly reported with anti-angiogenic agents.

EpidemiologyMean age at presentation ≈70 years; strong female predominance
Dose mattersLow-dose anti-resorptives (osteoporosis) → very low incidence. High-dose therapy (oncology) → substantially higher risk. Risk increases with duration of drug exposure
PresentationMost commonly exposed bone in the maxillofacial region; non-exposed variants (pain, fistula probing to bone) are recognised
DistributionMandible ≈65%, maxilla ≈28%, both jaws ≈6%
The risk is not uniform — and that is the clinically useful part

An osteoporosis patient on low-dose therapy has a very low incidence; an oncology patient on high-dose therapy has substantially higher risk. Treating both identically either denies routine care to the first group or under-protects the second. Dose, indication and duration are the questions to ask.

Back to Lecture 4

Healing and repair listed pathological fracture of the mandible as a recognised complication of MRONJ. And the mechanism connects directly to the remodelling cycle above: anti-resorptives suppress osteoclasts, so damaged bone is not removed and the coupled formation phase never follows.

Osteoradionecrosis of the jaw (ORN)

  • Area of exposed necrotic bone following radiation therapy that fails to heal for ≥3–6 months, in the absence of recurrent tumour
  • Most commonly affects the posterior mandible
  • Overall incidence with modern IMRT: ~4–5%
  • Common symptoms: pain, dysaesthesia, halitosis; a subset have intact mucosa with radiographic bone loss
MRONJ vs ORN

Both are non-healing exposed necrotic jaw bone. The distinction is the cause: MRONJ follows anti-resorptive (or anti-angiogenic) medication; ORN follows radiotherapy and requires the absence of recurrent tumour in the definition — because recurrent cancer is the main differential.

Why does the definition of ORN specifically exclude recurrent tumour?

Because in a previously irradiated field, recurrent malignancy is the critical differential diagnosis for non-healing bone — and the management is entirely different. Defining ORN as necrosis occurring in the absence of recurrent tumour forces that possibility to be excluded before the diagnosis is made, rather than assumed away.

09

Temporomandibular disorders

Where the biopsychosocial model replaced a mechanical one.

TMD

Pain and dysfunction of the TMJs and/or masticatory muscles. Prevalence 5–12% of the population in the USA, with 15% of these patients developing chronic TMD. Incidence ~4% per year, with half still experiencing symptoms 6 months later.

Aetiology: a model that changed

Historically, one-dimensional theories proposed a primary cause — TMJ, muscular, or occlusion.

Occlusion is not the cause

Good evidence suggests occlusal variables alone are not considered aetiologic factors in TMD. This overturns a long-held assumption, and it matters clinically: it is an argument against irreversible occlusal treatment for TMD.

Reade (1984) discussed TMD as a two-stage phenomenon — physical factors alone are insufficient. Engel (1977) proposed a biopsychosocial model of disease to address the social, psychological and behavioural dimensions of illness: biological, psychological and social factors together.

Risk factors

DomainFactors
PhysicalGender (W>M, only slightly); macrotrauma — wide opening for a long period (e.g. dental appointment, GA); clenching/bruxing; self-reported TMJ noises; parafunctional habits; genetics
PsychologicalHigh levels of depression, anxiety and perceived stress. Somatisation in up to ~77% and depression in up to ~60% of TMD patients. Frequency of somatic symptoms was the strongest psychosocial predictor
Other body painWidespread bodily pain, chronic headache/migraine, IBS, lower back pain, pelvic pain. Patients with the most severe TMD had the greatest burden of comorbid pain
General healthHistory of respiratory and neural conditions; 3+ medications; former or current smoking; poor sleep quality
A risk factor you create

Macrotrauma — wide opening for a long period, e.g. a dental appointment or general anaesthetic — is listed explicitly. Long procedures with the mouth held wide are a recognised precipitant, which is an argument for bite blocks and breaks in extended treatment.

Bruxism and sleep

Awake bruxism and sleep bruxism have biological, psychological and exogenous aetiology. The role of bruxism in the aetiology of myofascial pain/TMD is controversial, though many accept it as a risk factor. The proposed mechanism is that stress sensitivity and anxious personality traits may be responsible for bruxism, which may lead to temporomandibular pain, in turn modulated by psychosocial factors.

  • ~35% of the population complain of frequent sleep quality disturbance
  • Poor sleep is related to dysfunction in pain modulation pathways, important in pain perception
  • Poor sleep is a predictive factor for the onset of TMD; the OPPERA study found poor sleep quality contributed directly to the development of TMD, an association partially mediated by stress
Sleep links two halves of this lecture

Obstructive sleep apnoea destroys sleep quality; poor sleep quality predicts TMD onset. And mandibular advancement splints for OSA list jaw discomfort and TMJ discomfort among their side effects. The respiratory and musculoskeletal halves of this lecture meet at the mandible.

From the lecture slides
10

Diagnosing TMD, and joint disease

DC/TMD, disc displacement, and two arthritides.

DC/TMD

The biopsychosocial model was adapted into the RDC/TMD by Dworkin & LeResche (1992), which became the DC/TMD (2014).

  • Validated diagnostic criteria for TMD, good for research and clinical use
  • Non-hierarchical and allows for multiple diagnoses
  • Assessment via a dual-axis framework: Axis I — physical diagnosis; Axis II — psychosocial status and pain-related disability
Two axes, because one is not enough

Axis I records what is wrong with the joint and muscles. Axis II records the psychosocial dimension — and given somatisation in up to 77% and depression in up to 60% of TMD patients, a diagnosis that captures only Axis I misses much of what determines outcome.

Intra-articular TMDs

An intracapsular biomechanical disorder involving the condyle–disc complex. In the closed mouth position, the disc is in an anterior position relative to the condylar head. Disc displacements are most commonly anterior, followed by antero-lateral.

CategoryNote
Disc displacement with reductionRequires imaging / MRI for definitive diagnosis
Disc displacement with reduction and intermittent locking
Disc displacement without reduction, with limited opening
Disc displacement without reduction, without limited opening
“With reduction” means it goes back

In displacement with reduction, the disc is anterior at rest but returns onto the condyle during opening — producing the classic click. Without reduction, it never recaptures, so there may be no click but limited opening instead. Loss of a long-standing click accompanied by reduced opening is a meaningful change.

Osteoarthritis

Non-inflammatory focal degenerative disorder of synovial joints, primarily affecting articular cartilage and sub-condylar bone, initiated by deterioration of articular soft-tissue cover and exposure of bone.

Hypertrophic marginal osteophytes Subarticular cyst Subchondral sclerosis

Rheumatoid arthritis

A chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder, with inflammation of the synovial membrane characterised by oedema, cellular accumulation and synovial proliferation.

  • Breakdown of immunological self-tolerance
  • Mixed type III and type IV hypersensitivity reactions
  • Synoviocyte proliferation forming the destructive pannus
OA vs RA in one line

Osteoarthritis is non-inflammatory and focal — a wear-and-load problem in one joint. Rheumatoid arthritis is inflammatory and multisystem — an autoimmune disease that happens to attack synovium. That is why RA affects joints symmetrically and comes with systemic features, and OA does not.

Lecture 5, exactly

RA is named as mixed type III and type IV hypersensitivity following breakdown of immunological self-tolerance — the autoimmunity definition from L5B, using the effector mechanisms from L5A. It was also listed there among the major chronic disabling autoimmune diseases.

A patient's long-standing TMJ click has disappeared, but they can no longer open widely. Is this improvement?

No — it more likely represents progression from disc displacement with reduction to disc displacement without reduction, with limited opening. The click occurs as the anteriorly displaced disc recaptures onto the condyle during opening; if the disc no longer reduces, the click stops but the disc obstructs translation, limiting opening. Definitive diagnosis requires imaging / MRI.

11

Summary and glossary

Respiratory and musculoskeletal on one screen.

The through-line

  1. CO2 drives breathing
    Central chemoreceptors are primary; oxygen sensing is peripheral — which is why oxygen needs care in COPD.
  2. Mucociliary clearance is the recurring casualty
    Damaged in sinusitis, COPD and cystic fibrosis alike.
  3. Sinusitis and toothache mimic each other
    And ~25% of maxillary sinusitis has a dental cause.
  4. COPD is irreversible, asthma is reversible
    That single difference drives management.
  5. 80% of OSA is undiagnosed
    And its structural signs are all things a dentist examines routinely.
  6. Bone remodelling is coupled
    Osteoporosis uncouples it; anti-resorptives stall it, giving MRONJ.
  7. Occlusion alone does not cause TMD
    The biopsychosocial model replaced the mechanical one; sleep and psychological factors predict onset.
  8. OA is degenerative, RA is autoimmune
    Mixed type III and IV hypersensitivity after loss of self-tolerance.

Glossary

Mucociliary clearance
Coordinated upward ciliary beating removing inhaled particles.
Pseudostratified epithelium
Appears layered but all cells contact the basement membrane.
Central chemoreceptors
Medullary receptors responding to CO₂ and H⁺; the primary drivers of ventilation.
Haemoptysis
Blood in the sputum.
Purulent sputum
Thick yellow–green sputum indicating a neutrophil-rich exudate.
CFTR
The protein defective in cystic fibrosis, causing thick mucus and recurrent infection.
α-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Unopposed neutrophil elastase causing early-onset emphysema.
COPD
Chronic bronchitis and emphysema; irreversible airflow obstruction on expiration.
Asthma
Intermittent airway hyperactivity with a reversible obstructive component.
Apnoea
Drop in peak signal excursion ≥90% of baseline for ≥10 seconds.
Hypopnoea
A lesser reduction in airflow with desaturation or arousal.
CPAP
Continuous positive airway pressure; a pneumatic splint and the gold standard for OSA.
MAS / MAD
Mandibular advancement splint/device; second-line OSA therapy with better compliance.
Basic multicellular unit
The organised group of cells carrying out a remodelling cycle.
Osteoblast / osteoclast / osteocyte
Bone-forming, bone-resorbing, and strain-sensing cells.
Coupling
The normal balance of resorption and formation within a remodelling unit.
Osteoporosis
Reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation; resorption exceeds formation.
MRONJ
Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, from anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic drugs.
ORN
Osteoradionecrosis — exposed necrotic bone after radiotherapy failing to heal for ≥3–6 months, without recurrent tumour.
TMD
Pain and dysfunction of the TMJs and/or masticatory muscles.
Biopsychosocial model
Engel's framework addressing biological, psychological and social dimensions of illness.
DC/TMD
Validated dual-axis diagnostic criteria for TMD; Axis I physical, Axis II psychosocial.
Disc displacement with reduction
The disc is anterior at rest but recaptures on opening, producing a click.
Pannus
Proliferating inflamed synovium that destroys joint structures in rheumatoid arthritis.
Required reading

Underwood’s Pathology: a Clinical Approach (8th ed.), Simon Cross (2024). The lecture also cites Okeson 2020, Schiffman et al. 2014, Suvinen et al. 2005, Manfredini et al. 2017, Sanders et al. 2013 and 2017, and the OPPERA studies.
